scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Zebola originated in the folklore groups of Kintambo, Kinshasa, in the 1970s.
It was brought into the mainstream by Zaïko Langa Langa in 1982, specifically through the performances of Bébé Atalaku and Nono Monzuluku.
on_screen: Map: Democratic Republic of the Congo · Africa

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Zebola is performed during the sebene section of Congolese rumba songs.
It is used to excite the audience and prompt them to dance, while also serving as a way to reference patrons and performers.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
on_screen: Formation: Often involves joining choreographed dance formations on stage, sometimes leading the front dance line.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is defined by the sebene section of Congolese rumba, characterized by fast-paced guitar riffs and drum rhythms.
The atalaku uses a spray can shaker to amplify the percussive rhythm.
Listen for the spray can shaker, guitar, snare drum.
The sound is defined by an accelerated guitar riff following the chorus, accompanied by the percussive rattle of a spray can shaker and the rhythmic, improvisational shouts of the atalaku.

Derived from the folklore ('urban traditional') music of Kintambo, Kinshasa, and integrated into modern Congolese rumba.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Some traditionalists viewed the incorporation of this folklore as inappropriate for modern popular music, noting it was better suited to ceremonial and ritual settings.
